Members of environmental organizations reported being just as altruistic (assessed with the Self-Report Altruism Scale; Rushton et al., 1981) as members of humanitarian organizations. Yet only members of environmental organizations expressed higher pro-environmental attitudes. Taken together, these findings suggest that caring about nature implies caring about people, whereas caring about people does not imply caring about nature to the same degree.

So far, little attention has been paid to these emerging asymmetries. If we summarize the extant research, it is reasonable to describe the relation between altruistic and biospheric values as a persistent correlation. Biospheric values are distinct from altruistic values, yet still closely associated. A correlation can, by definition, only demonstrate a bidirectional (that is, symmetrical) association. However, characterizing this as a symmetrical correlation may obscure the structural relationship between biospheric and altruistic values. For example, it could be presumed from a symmetrical understanding that biospheric values should predict altruistic behavior approximately as well as altruistic values predict environmental behaviorwhich seems not to be the case. Thus, existing accounts of the structure of altruistic and biospheric values lack a theoretical rationale to explain the asymmetries we observe in the literature. Next, we outline a theoretical model that explains these asymmetries.

1.4 The inclusion model

We propose that biospheric values inherently include altruistic values. We draw from Schultz's (2001) work on the structure of environmental concern, specifically, the Inclusion Model of Environmental Concern, which describes environmental concern as concentric circles of an expanding self. Schultz argues that individuals may care about environmental issues because of their impact on the self (egoistic environmental concern), on others (altruistic environmental concern), or on the biosphere itself (biospheric environmental concern). Anyone will care about environmental harm if it is personally relevant. An individual concerned about environmental issues because of their impact on other humans will still hold some level of egoistic environmental concern. Someone concerned about the environment for the environment's sake will also care out of concern for other humans and for the self (Milfont & Schultz, 2018; Nolan & Schultz, 2015).

De Dominicis and colleagues (2017) present a compelling empirical test of the Inclusion Model of Environmental Concern. They examined message framing to encourage environmental volunteering. They found that individuals high in egoistic environmental concern were more likely to sign up for an environmental volunteering activity when exposed to a self-enhancing message and given a monetary incentive, compared with a selftranscendent appeal. In contrast, individuals high in biospheric environmental concern were equally likely to sign up for an environmental volunteering activity regardless of the message framing. The authors concluded that biospheric environmental concern includes egoistic environmental concern, but not vice versa.

We extend Schultz's (2001) Inclusion Model of Environmental Concern to explain the structure of altruistic and biospheric values. Biospheric values contain an altruistic core, shared with altruistic values. This extension differs from Schultz's original model in two respects. The original model describes three reasons why people are concerned about the environment (egoistic, altruistic, and biospheric environmental concern), nested in an inclusion structure. In contrast, the extended model we present here focuses solely on the relation between altruistic and biospheric values and proposes an inclusion structure to describe this relationship. See Figure 1A for a visualization of the proposed extended inclusion model (hereafter, when we refer to the inclusion model, we mean this extended version).

It is reasonable to expect that the inclusive structure extends from environmental concern to values. Otto and colleagues (2021) theorize that biospheric motivation is partly based on altruism. Specifically, they argue altruistic motivations share a common core (i.e., concern for humans) with biospheric motivations (see also Frank et al., 2024; Neef et al., 2026). Similarly, Hilbig and colleagues (2013) show that environmental behavior depends on people's willingness to cooperate with others. Note. Panel A depicts the proposed inclusion model. Panel B depicts the non-inclusion correlated account, while Panel C depicts the non-inclusion unidimensional account. The two symmetrical accounts (B and C) differ conceptually only in the size of the overlap between the two circles.

Beyond this support from prior work, there is also a theoretical rationale for why biospheric values should encompass altruistic values. Altruistic values and biospheric values are both expressions of broader self-transcendent values (de Groot & Steg, 2007; Schultz et al., 2005). Both motivate action to help entities beyond the self, but the target of help differs. Nolan and Schultz (2015) invoke parallels between the Inclusion Model of Environmental Concern and work on the scope of justice (Opotow, 1993; Opotow & Clayton, 1994). Individuals with a broader scope of justice will care for the welfare of more distant entities, such as other people and aspects of nature. Others argue that including more distant entities (such as elements of the natural world) within one's scope of justice entails including less distant entities like other people (Castelo et al., 2021; Crimston et al., 2016). Individuals motivated to help the planet can be thought of as having the broadest conception of the self, one that includes the environment and other people. This may influence how the motivational target of self-transcendent values manifests, where helping nature also means helping others.

Another explanation for an inclusion pattern of values may be purely associative.

Social and environmental action are not mutually exclusive, and many individuals may associate the two. Song and colleagues (2020) found that individuals who were more familiar with the topic of environmental justice were more likely to draw a connection between social and environmental issues. Sustainability research frequently acknowledges the interplay between environmental and social justice issues (Raworth, 2017; World Commission on Environment and Development [WCED], 1987). Few environmental issues are without social implications, while many humanitarian issues lack a clear connection to environmental problems. This suggests an inherent asymmetry in cognitive associations between environmental and social issues, which may, in turn, shape how altruistic and biospheric values develop among those who care about the environment.

1.4.1 Hypotheses

To test the inclusion model, we derive three hypotheses. Each hypothesis reflects an empirical expectation of the inclusion model that distinguishes it from competing theoretical explanations, in line with Platt (1964). Specifically, we test our proposed asymmetric inclusion model against the symmetric, correlated account, and the unidimensional account (see Figure 1).

If biospheric values include altruistic values, this should be visible in how people endorse the two values. Endorsing biospheric values should imply endorsing altruistic values, while endorsing altruistic values should not imply endorsing biospheric values to the same extent.

H1: People who strongly endorse biospheric values also strongly endorse altruistic values, whereas the reverse holds to a lesser degree (i.e., biospheric-only endorsement is less common than altruistic-only endorsement).

The same asymmetry should be reflected in the outcomes the two values predict.

Because only biospheric values include concern for the non-human world, they should be more closely linked to environmental outcomes compared to altruistic values. However, since both values share concern for other people, they should be more similarly linked to humanitarian outcomes.

H2: Biospheric values predict environmental outcomes more strongly than altruistic values (H2a), whereas both values predict humanitarian outcomes approximately equally well (H2b).

According to the inclusion model, biospheric values comprise two components: an altruistic core, reflecting concern for other people, which they share with altruistic values, and a biospheric-specific element, reflecting concern for the non-human world. This structure should also be reflected in how the two values relate at the latent level. Beyond these hypotheses, we aim to illustrate the practical benefit of the inclusion model. When both correlated values are entered together as predictors, suppression effects can distort their estimated relationships with outcomes (see Akinwande et al., 2015; Patrick et al., 2007). For instance, when entering both values in a multiple regression, de Groot and Steg (2008) found that altruistic values negatively predicted an environmental outcome, despite being unrelated to it at the bivariate level (see also Katz-Gerro et al., 2017). We examine whether modeling the two values in line with the inclusion model avoids such distortions and yields more interpretable relationships with outcomes.

2 Methods

We tested our hypotheses in three complementary studies. Studies 1 and 2 test all three hypotheses (H1-H3). Study 3 tested only H1 and H2, as the available data did not allow a test of H3. Study 2 was preregistered. Study 1 uses data originally collected for another project, and Study 3 uses secondary data from two large global datasets. As Studies 1 and 3 used preexisting data, our analyses were not preregistered; however, our analysis files are publicly available. Deviations from the preregistration for Study 2 are reported in the Supplementary Materials.

Studies 1 and 2 were deemed exempt from ethical approval by the Institutional Review Board of the [anonymous]. Study 3 used secondary data, so it did not require ethical approval. We conducted analyses in RStudio (Posit Team, 2025). All data, analysis code, and our surveys for Studies 1 and 2 are available on OSF (https://osf.io/qywj2/overview?view_only=a17631fc20014608a26eab594ca0f4fa).

Alphanumerically referenced tables and figures can be found in the Supplementary Materials.

2.1 Participants

2.1.1 Participants Study 1

We collected the data for Study 1 as part of another project, in partnership with VolunteerMatch (now Idealist), a non-profit that aggregates volunteer opportunities across the United States. The sample represents American volunteers, rather than the general population; however, this population is of interest as they likely hold stronger biospheric and altruistic values than the general population. The data used here were supplementary measures from the first wave of a two-wave study. Participants were volunteers from across the United States, and 248 completed the survey. We removed 26 participants under the age of 18, resulting in a final sample of N = 222 (74.2% Female, <1% Non-binary). Participants were, on average, 51.4 years old (SD = 16.8, range: 19-86).

2.1.2 Participants Study 2

Participants were recruited via Prolific. Participants received a standard payment of £0.90 for the entire study. They were selected to represent the U.S. population in terms of age, gender, ethnicity, and political orientation, and we initially collected 817 participants.

Adhering to our preregistered data-exclusion criteria, we removed n = 24 for failing the attention check item embedded within the value survey (an instructed response item; Meade & Craig, 2012; see OSF), n = 1 for missing more than 25% of responses, and n = 1 for taking too long to complete the survey (longer than 93 hours). The final sample consisted of N = 791 participants (48.5% Female, 2% Non-binary). Participants were, on average, 44.9 years old (SD = 15.8; range: 18-84). Our sample exceeded the a priori calculated minimum sample size of 785 to detect a small correlation (r = .10) with power = .80 and α = .05.

2.1.3 Participants Study 3

We used nationally representative data from the World Values Survey (WVS) and the European Social Survey (ESS), two multinational surveys conducted in several waves. The data are freely accessible. We used Round 6 of the WVS, conducted between 2010 and 2014 (Inglehart et al., 2014), and Round 11 of the ESS (European Social Survey European Research Infrastructure [ESS ERIC], 2025). In total, N = 85,796 individuals from C = 52 different countries answered the variables included in our analysis. Each country contributed between 663 and 3,462 participants (M = 1,574).

2.1 Measures

2.1.1 Measures in Studies 1 and 2

To measure altruistic and biospheric values, participants completed Steg and colleagues' (2014) values questionnaire. They rated the importance of 16 values "as a guiding principle" in their lives (-1 = opposed to my values,0 = not important at all,6 = very important,7 = one of my most important values). These values represent altruistic (four items), biospheric (four items), hedonic (three items), and egoistic value orientation (five items). We used only altruistic and biospheric values in our analyses. Internal consistencies for altruistic values were αStudy1 = .70 and αStudy2 = .82. For biospheric values, the internal consistencies were αStudy1 = .86 and αStudy2 = .92. The correlation between both values were rStudy1 = .42 (95% CI[.31, .52]) and rStudy2 = .65 (95% CI[.61, .69]). Study 1 additionally included Schultz's (2001) environmental concern scale, which was used for a supplementary robustness check of the inclusion model with a non-values measure of motivation (see Section 4.3 and Table S.1).

Study 1 included two dependent variables assessing self-reported behavior: humanitarian and environmental volunteering. Participants indicated which types of volunteering causes they had participated in during the last year (based on the "cause areas" listed on the VolunteerMatch website). If participants volunteered in humanitarian causes (e.g., serving as a court-appointed child foster care advocate), they received a 1 in humanitarian volunteering (or a 0 for not participating). The same coding applies to volunteering for environmental causes (e.g., planting trees).

Study 2 included four dependent variables. To obtain the first set of two variables, participants read a scenario in which they imagined themselves as a city council member deciding whether to reallocate half of a surplus budget (previously used for tax relief for local residents) toward alternative community initiatives. They were told that an independent consultancy had identified all initiatives as high-need priorities that approximately cost the same. Participants then completed a series of forced-choice trials, each presenting a 7-point preference scale between the tax relief policy (designed to tap into egoistic values) and one of six alternative proposals: three environmental ("reforesting unused plots of land," "creating a local organic gardening/farming initiative," and "installing solar panels on local public buildings") and three altruistic ("building a new community playground," "creating a community center for the elderly," and "creating a youth center"). From these trials, we derived two preference indices per participant: average preference for altruistic alternatives over tax relief and average preference for environmental alternatives over tax relief (αaltruistic = .86; αbiospheric = .87). The full measure and information on a pilot test with 51 participants are available in Table S.2.

As a second set of dependent variables, participants completed an incentivized allocation task, choosing between an additional personal payment of £0.10 or a charitable donation of £0.01-£0.10. Participants were randomly assigned to either an environmental (Natural Resources Defense Council) or a humanitarian charity (World Central Kitchen) condition to prevent the two causes from competing. Means and SDs for all variables included are reported in Table S.3.

2.1.4 Measures in Study 3

Study 3 combined the ESS (Round 11) and the WVS (Round 6) data. Both surveys include items that closely resemble altruistic and biospheric values and have been used as proxies for these values in previous research (see Law et al., 2025; Martin, 2023). The ESS and the WVS measure values with items from Schwartz's theory of basic values (Schwartz, 1992 (Schwartz, , 2003)), in which respondents are presented with short portraits of a hypothetical person and indicate how similar this person is to themselves (recorded on a six-point Likert-type scale ranging from 1 ["very much like me"] to 6 ["not at all like me"]).

In Round 6 of the WVS, biospheric values were captured by one universalism item ("Looking after the environment is important to this person; to care for nature and save life resources."; item code in the WVS: V78) and altruistic values by one benevolence item ("It is important for this person to help the people nearby; to care for their well-being."; item code in the WVS: V74B). Note that, because this benevolence item was not available in all WVS countries, some countries, such as the United States, were not included.

In Round 11 of the ESS, biospheric values were likewise captured by a universalism item similar to the WVS ("She/he strongly believes that people should care for nature.

Looking after the environment is important to her/him."; item code in the ESS: impenva).

Altruistic values were measured with one benevolence item ("It's very important to her/him to help the people around her/him. She/he wants to care for their well-being."; item code in the ESS: iphlppla) and one universalism item ("She/he thinks it is important that every person in the world should be treated equally. She/he believes everyone should have equal opportunities in life."; item code in the ESS: ipeqopta). We averaged these two items. We reverse-coded all value items so that higher numerical values indicate stronger endorsement of the respective value orientation.

We searched the WVS and ESS datasets for suitable outcome variables. The only outcomes measured for both the humanitarian and environmental domains were membership in an environmental organization (item code in the WVS: V30) and membership in a humanitarian or charitable organization (item code in the WVS: V32), both of which we coded as 0 (no membership) or 1 (passive or active membership). The other potential outcomes in the WVS and ESS either did not distinguish between the environmental and the humanitarian domain or covered only one of them.

2.2 Analytic strategy

2.2.1 H1: Asymmetry in the co-occurrence of value orientations in Studies 1 to 3

Our first test of the inclusion model focused on the co-occurrence of both values within individuals. According to the inclusion model, caring about the environment implies caring about peoplebut not necessarily the other way around. To test the inclusion model, we dichotomized participants' value scores into endorsement (1) or non-endorsement (0), borrowing this approach from Kaiser and Byrka (2011). In Studies 1 and 2, where values were measured on a -1 to 7 scale, we defined non-endorsement as a score of -1 to < 6 and endorsement as a score of 6 to 7 (preregistered in Study 2). Study 3 used ad hoc items on a 1-6 scale, so we split at the natural midpoint (1-3 = non-endorsement; 4-6 = endorsement; note that the two-item altruistic value measure in the ESS was rounded prior to dichotomization).

We used a fixed, scale-based threshold rather than a sample-based split (e.g., a median split) for two reasons. First, we aimed to classify participants based on their absolute standing on the response scale rather than on their position relative to others. Second, a median split would force roughly equal proportions of endorsers for both values, which would prevent detection of an asymmetric co-occurrence pattern.

From these dichotomized indicators, we constructed 22 contingency tables capturing the joint distribution of altruistic and biospheric value endorsement. The inclusion model's key prediction concerns the discordant casesthose endorsing one value but not the other valuemaking McNemar's test the appropriate analytic tool (Agresti, 2002). We also report the matched-pairs odds ratio as an effect size, quantifying the relative likelihood of the two discordant patterns.

To examine whether the inclusion account holds across different global regions in Study 3, we grouped countries into eight macroregions. European countries were divided into four sub-regions: Northern Europe (e.g., Estonia, Sweden), Western Europe (e.g., France, Germany), Southern Europe (e.g., Greece, Italy), and Eastern Europe (e.g., Bulgaria, Ukraine). We grouped non-European countries into four additional regions: Latin America (e.g., Brazil, Colombia), Middle East and North Africa (MENA; e.g., Egypt, Iraq), sub-Saharan Africa (e.g., Rwanda, South Africa), and East Asia (e.g., China, Japan). The full country list is reported in Table S.4. We repeated the analyses described above for each macroregion. 1As robustness checks, we applied two alternative dichotomization cutoffs in all three studies. In Study 3, we additionally examined the co-occurrence pattern in each country.

These analyses yielded largely consistent results (see Tables S.5 and S.6).

2.2.2 H2: Asymmetry in predicting relevant outcomes in Studies 1 to 3

The second key prediction of the inclusion model is that biospheric values should predict environmental outcomes better than altruistic values do. In contrast, for humanitarian outcomes, both values should predict comparably well. To test this, we compared the predictive strength of the two values for each pair of humanitarian and environmental outcomes in our studies. The outcomes were humanitarian and environmental volunteering (Study 1), preferences for humanitarian and environmental budget proposals (Study 2), an incentivized donation to a humanitarian or an environmental charity (Study 2), and humanitarian and environmental organizational membership (Study 3). In Studies 1 and 2, we computed value indices by averaging across the respective items. All value measures were zstandardized (Fischer & Milfont, 2010).

For volunteering (Study 1), preferences (Study 2), and organizational membership (Study 3), each participant provided both humanitarian and environmental outcomes. We therefore analyzed both outcomes in one model per sample, including outcome type (humanitarian vs. environmental), both values, and their interaction. To account for the two observations per participant, we used cluster-robust standard errors (Zeileis, 2006). For the binary outcomes (volunteering and membership), we estimated logistic regression models. In Study 3 (membership), we ran the models separately in each macroregion, as in the cooccurrence analysis. 2 For preferences, we estimated linear regression models. We then tested H2a and H2b by comparing the slopes of the two values within each outcome type using simple-slope contrasts.

We analyzed incentivized donations differently because each participant donated to only one target (humanitarian or environmental). We estimated separate linear regression models for the two subsamples and compared the coefficients of the two values within each.

Because donations were strongly non-normally distributed, with clusters at no, medium, and full donation, we used heteroscedasticity-consistent standard errors.

None of the models included covariates. As robustness checks, we re-estimated all models with age, gender, education, and income as covariates (see Table S.7). In Study 3, we additionally included country as a fixed effect in each macroregion model (see Table S.8) and estimated the models separately for each country (see Table S.9). These analyses yielded results consistent with the main analyses.

2.2.3 H3: Confirmatory factor analyses in Studies 1 and 2

To test H3a and H3b, we represented the inclusion model as a bifactor-(S-1) model (Eid, 2020; Eid et al., 2017; see Figure 2). The bifactor-(S-1) model is designed for correlated constructs that share a common element, making it suitable for modeling altruistic and biospheric values in line with our proposed inclusion model. Bifactor-(S-1) models consist of a general factor (G) and specific factors that are orthogonal to G. All items load on G. Items from one domain only load onto G, while items from all other domains load onto both G and a specific factor. Here, G represents the shared core altruistic element shared by both types of values, and the second factor represents the element specific to biospheric values (Bio-s). Eid (2020) recommends choosing the domain that loads only onto G on theoretical grounds, since it defines the interpretation of the model. As the inclusion model posits that altruistic concern is shared by both value orientations, we chose altruistic items as the reference domain (see Nolan & Schultz, 2015; Schultz, 2001). This structure aligns with the understanding that people may endorse biospheric values partly out of concern for other humans. The reverse structure (where altruistic values would consist of a biospheric core and an altruism-specific element) seems less theoretically plausible, as it implies that both types of values share, at their core, concern for the natural world. For completeness, however, we also specified such a model, in which the biospheric items define the general factor and the altruistic items additionally load on an altruisticspecific factor. In essence, this is the mirror image of the bifactor-(S-1) inclusion model.

Using confirmatory factor analysis, we compared the bifactor-(S-1) inclusion model to two established alternatives. The first corresponds to the correlated understanding (two correlated factors for their respective items). The second corresponds to a unidimensional understanding of the two values (a single factor for all items). 2.2.4 Structural equation models in Studies 1 and 2

We used the bifactor-(S-1) model to illustrate the practical value of the inclusion model (i.e., to overcome typical interpretational challenges arising from the overlap between the two values; Moshagen, 2023). By introducing relevant outcomes, the bifactor-(S-1) model becomes a structural equation model (SEM; see Eid et al., 2018). These outcomes were volunteering (Study 1), policy preferences (Study 2), and incentivized donation (Study 2). For the donation, we estimated separate SEMs for the two donation subsamples. No SEMs were estimated for Study 3, as values were measured with single-or two-item proxies. In all SEMs, we regressed both humanitarian and environmental outcomes on the altruistic core and the biospheric-specific factor.

3 Results

We present our results in four sections. First, we report the asymmetric co-occurrence of the two values across Studies 1 to 3 (H1). Second, we report the predictive asymmetry across Studies 1 to 3 (H2). Third, we test the latent structure of the two values in Studies 1 and 2 (H3). Finally, we demonstrate the practical usefulness of modeling data in line with the inclusion model using SEMs.

3.1 H1: Asymmetry in the co-occurrence of value orientations in Studies 1 to 3

Across all samples, strongly endorsing biospheric values largely implied strongly endorsing altruistic values, whereas strongly endorsing altruistic values implied strongly endorsing biospheric values to a considerably lesser extent (see Table 1 and Figure 3). This is evident in the fact that the share of individuals who endorsed only biospheric values (range: 1.4-10.8%) was smaller than the share who endorsed only altruistic values (range: 7.2-25.2%) in every sample.

McNemar's tests confirmed that this difference was consistently significant. Only the strength of asymmetry varied. It was more pronounced in the U.S.

(Studies 1 and 2), Europe, and Latin America (Study 3; ORs = 1.95-5.28), and less pronounced in MENA, sub-Saharan Africa, and East Asia (ORs = 1.35-1.61). Nevertheless, samples from all three studies support H1. Asymmetry in Altruistic and Biospheric Value Endorsement Across Different World Regions Note. Colors reflect the Odds Ratio (OR) of endorsing altruistic but not biospheric values relative to endorsing biospheric but not altruistic values. OR > 1 (green) indicates that altruisticonly endorsement is more prevalent than biospheric-only endorsement, consistent with the inclusion model. European regions (N = 47,929; 29 countries) are based on the European Social Survey (Round 11); All non-European regions but the United States (N = 33,903; 23 countries) are based on the World Values Survey (Round 6). United States is based on Study 2.3.2 H2: Asymmetry in predicting relevant outcomes in Studies 1 to 3 Figure 4 shows the predictive strength of both values for environmental outcomes (left panels) and humanitarian outcomes (right panels) across all samples and outcomes, with both values entered simultaneously as predictors in multiple regression models (see also Tables S.10 and S.11). The expected pattern from the inclusion model is that the green line (biospheric values) should be steeper than the black dashed line (altruistic values) in the left, environmental panels (H2a), whereas both lines should be similarly steep in the right, humanitarian panels (H2b). At first glance, this pattern is visible in most samples.

In Study 1 (Panel A), biospheric values strongly and positively predicted environmental volunteering, whereas altruistic values did not. The difference between the two slopes was significant (z = 3.15, p = .002). For humanitarian volunteering, both slopes were positive and almost parallel and did not differ (z = 0.52, p = .606). Finally, Panel A shows the anticipated suppression effect (see Section 1.4.1). On their own, altruistic values were unrelated to environmental volunteering (b = -0.07, p = .621), but they were negatively related to it once biospheric values were included in the model (b = -0.37, p = .033).

In Study 2 (Panel B), biospheric values again predicted environmental preferences more strongly than altruistic values did (t = 2.83, p = .005), whereas both values predicted humanitarian preferences to a similar extent (t = 1.78, p = .076).

The results looked different for the incentivized donation (Panel C). Here, the two lines for environmental donations were nearly parallel, and biospheric values were not a significantly stronger predictor (F = 0.67, p = .506). For humanitarian donations, only altruistic values predicted donations, whereas biospheric values did not (b = 0.05, p = .851), and the two slopes differed significantly (F = 5.66, p = .018). However, biospheric values alone predicted humanitarian donations (b = 0.91, p < .001). As for volunteering in Study 1, the association of one value with the outcome changed substantially once the other value was taken into account, reflecting the overlap between the two values.

Finally, turning to Study 3 (Panels D-H), the left panels show that biospheric values predicted membership in an environmental organization more strongly than altruistic values in Europe (z = 6.87, p < .001), Latin America (z = 6.91, p < .001), MENA (z = 3.31, p = .001), and sub-Saharan Africa (z = 5.62, p < .001). In East Asia, the difference pointed in the same direction but was not significant (z = 1.75, p = .081). In the right panels, the two values predicted membership in a humanitarian organization similarly well in Europe (z = -1.41, p = .159), MENA (z = -1.24, p = .214), and East Asia (z = 0.58, p = .563). In Latin America (z = -3.21, p = .001) and sub-Saharan Africa (z = -3.71, p < .001), however, biospheric values were the stronger predictor, even of humanitarian membership. Across Studies 1 to 3 Note. The panels show predicted volunteering (Panel A), preferences (Panel B), donations (Panel C), and organizational membership (org. mem. ; Panels D-H). In Panel C, environmental and humanitarian donations come from two separate subsamples. Shaded areas are 95% CIs. WVS = World Values Survey; MENA = Middle East and North Africa.

Taken together, H2a was supported for all outcomes and samples except donations (Study 2), with a nonsignificant difference in East Asia (although the results were in the expected direction). H2b was supported for all outcomes and samples except donations (Study 2), Latin America, and sub-Saharan Africa. The full predicted asymmetry thus emerged for volunteering (Study 1), preferences (Study 2), and in Europe and MENA (Study 3), and descriptively in East Asia. The remaining deviations, however, differed in how strongly they contradict the inclusion model. In Latin America and sub-Saharan Africa, biospheric values were the stronger predictor of both outcomes, so their predicted advantage for environmental outcomes still held.

For donations, in contrast, no part of the predicted asymmetry was supported.

3.3 H3: Confirmatory factor analyses in Studies 1 and 2

In our final set of hypothesis tests, we return to Studies 1 and 2, which measured values using Steg and colleagues's (2014) full scale. We examined whether a latent representation of the inclusion model fit better than a correlated two-factor model ( H3a) and a unidimensional model (H3b). Table 2 presents the fit of all three models, together with the mirror-image model estimated as an additional analysis (see Tables S.12 and S.13 for full models, including factor loadings).

In both studies, the bifactor-(S-1) model fit the data considerably better than the unidimensional model on all fit indices. Its advantage over the correlated two-factor model was smaller. In Study 1, the two models fit almost equally well, with CFI and SRMR slightly favoring the bifactor-(S-1) model and TLI and RMSEA slightly favoring the correlated twofactor model. In Study 2, the bifactor-(S-1) model fit better on all fit indices, though not by a large margin.

The mirror-image model fit better than the inclusion model in Study 1, but worse in Study 2. In Study 1, this difference could be traced to poor fit of a single altruistic value item ("helpful"), which loaded weakly on the general factor when this factor was defined by the biospheric items (λ = .16). When this item was excluded, the fit comparison favored the inclusion model again (see Supplementary Material). However, comparing the two bifactor specifications is generally of limited use. Both share the same structure and differ only in which items define the general factor. Each captures item heterogeneity within a given domain differently (Eid et al., 2017), so differences in fit do not necessarily indicate a theoretically more meaningful specification. This highlights the importance of choosing a bifactor-(S-1) model specification based on theoretical, rather than empirical, standing, as Eid (2020) recommends (see also Supplementary Material). Note. Models were estimated using the weighted least squares mean-and variance-adjusted estimator; scaled test statistics and fit indices are reported. Mirror-image bifactor-(S-1) models (in italics) were estimated as an additional analysis. Relatively high RMSEA values are likely explained by low degrees of freedom (Kenny et al., 2015).

In sum, the bifactor-(S-1) model fit at least as well as the correlated two-factor model, partially supporting H3a, and better than the unidimensional model, supporting H3b.

However, the main advantage of the bifactor-(S-1) inclusion model is the interpretational clarity it provides. We illustrate this in the following final results section.

3.4 Structural equation models in Studies 1 and 2

In Section 3.2, the overlap between the two values made some regression results difficult to interpret. In Study 1, altruistic values were negatively related to environmental volunteering only after we included biospheric values in the model (i.e., suppression). For humanitarian donations in Study 2, the association with biospheric values disappeared once altruistic values were included. Decomposing biospheric values into an altruistic core and an uncorrelated biospheric-specific factor can clarify such patterns. We therefore extended the bifactor-(S-1) model into SEMs for each outcome (see Eid et al., 2018), which all showed acceptable fit (see Figure 5).

The SEMs revealed a consistent pattern across outcomes. The altruistic core (G) predicted all humanitarian outcomes and, except for volunteering, also environmental outcomes.

In contrast, the biospheric-specific factor (Bio-s) predicted only environmental outcomes and was unrelated to humanitarian volunteering, preferences, and donations. This also means that, in Study 1, the altruistic core was not negatively related to environmental volunteering. In other words, the suppression effect observed in the regression model (Figure 4, Panel A) did not appear. Similarly, for donations (Study 2), humanitarian donations depended only on the altruistic core, consistent with the finding that biospheric values predicted them alone but not after altruistic values were taken into account (Figure 4, Panel C). More concretely, the positive zero-order relation between biospheric values and humanitarian donations was now captured by the altruistic core shared by both values. In addition, the biospheric-specific factor uniquely predicted environmental donations. Predicting Outcomes in Studies 1 and 2 Note. *** p < .001, ** p < .01, * p < .05. 4 Discussion

4.1 Summary of the results

Across samples, people who strongly endorsed biospheric values also tended to strongly endorse altruistic values, whereas people who strongly endorsed altruistic values were less likely to strongly endorse biospheric values (H1). Second, in most samples, biospheric values predicted environmental outcomes better than altruistic values (H2a), whereas both values predicted humanitarian outcomes similarly well (H2b). Third, modeling the inclusion model as a latent structure where biospheric values contain an altruistic core and a biosphere-specific component performed well. The latent bifactor-(S-1) inclusion model fit the data slightly better than a latent structure with the two values as distinct but correlated and fit considerably better than a latent structure with them as a single dimension (H3a and H3b).

Table 3 summarizes empirical tests and results across all studies. Still, not all findings matched our predictions. The clearest divergence concerned the incentivized donations in Study 2. Here, biospheric values did not predict environmental donations better than altruistic values, while altruistic values predicted humanitarian donations better than biospheric values. This altruistic advantage, however, was particularly pronounced when both values were entered simultaneously in a regression (see Figure 4; Panel C). On their own, both values were positively related to humanitarian donations (altruistic: r = .30; biospheric: r = .20), whereas biospheric values were unrelated once altruistic values were accounted for. It is harder to explain why biospheric values failed to predict environmental donations better than altruistic values. One possible explanation lies in the environmental charity we chose. It is possible that participants did not perceive the environmental charity we selected (The Natural Resources Defense Council) as favorably or as strictly an environmental cause. Another explanation could be that altruistic values are more consistently associated with charity donations (see Lohmann et al., 2024; but see also de

Groot & Steg, 2010; Lundberg et al., 2019).

Beyond donations, our findings showed some heterogeneity across world regions. In East Asia, an asymmetric prediction pattern could be observed descriptively, but only one contrast was significant. One possible explanation is that many East Asian cultural traditions (e.g., Japan) draw less sharp a distinction between humans and the natural world (Tateishi et al., 2026; see also Yu & Reiss, 2025). If protecting the natural world inherently means protecting others, biospheric values may offer little advantage over altruistic values in predicting environmental outcomes. In Latin America and sub-Saharan Africa, biospheric values predicted not only environmental but also humanitarian membership better than altruistic values. This may partly reflect that some humanitarian organizations in these regions also have environmental aims, as social initiatives often arise in direct response to the social harms of environmental issues such as extractivism (Munck, 2020; Obi, 2005). More generally, global heterogeneity could stem in part from cultural differences in human-nature schemas or reflect the limitations of Western conceptions of humanitarian and environmental issues (Banerjee, 2003; Cronon, 1996; Yu & Reiss, 2025).

Although the inclusion model did not hold equally across all tests, it still received stronger support than the two alternative accounts. Both a unidimensional and a correlated model would require additional assumptions to explain the observed asymmetric cooccurrence. A unidimensional account would have to assume that biospheric values are the more "difficult" expression of the same underlying orientation. A correlated account would have to assume that biospheric values are consistently less prevalent than altruistic values (see Schwartz & Bardi, 2001), but it offers little theoretical reason why this prevalence difference should run in the same direction across all regions. Neither non-inclusive account explains the predominant predictive asymmetry. A unidimensional account does not accommodate differences in predictive ability. Any symmetrical account would expect altruistic values to predict humanitarian outcomes better than biospheric values, which was generally not the case here. Moreover, the inclusion model fit the data better than a unidimensional model and fit at least as well as a correlated model. We conclude that the inclusion model best explains the overall pattern of findings.

4.2 Implications for theory and research

The inclusion model aligns well with other lay conceptualizations from sustainability literature, where caring for the natural environment implies caring for people, but caring for people does not always mean caring for the environment (Österblom & Paasche, 2021; WCED, 1987). Psychologically, this asymmetry can be understood as expanding circles of care. Those who include nature within the bounds of their concern already include others within it (see Crimston et al., 2016; Opotow, 1993; Opotow & Clayton, 1994).

Therefore, biospheric values explain humanitarian outcomes about equally well as altruistic values, while altruistic values often fail to explain environmental outcomes. This interpretation finds empirical support in past literature (see Kaiser & Byrka, 2011) and helps explain why broad prosocial (i.e., other-related) constructs, such as trait altruism or Honesty-Humility, are consistently related to various forms of biospheric motivations and behavior (e.g., Drosinou et al., 2025; Otto et al., 2021). Indeed, in line with our work, these prosocial constructs overlap conceptually with biospheric motivations.

While we present the argument for the inclusion model using data on biospheric and altruistic values, this model may extend to other forms of motivation as well. Values can be understood as a form of motivation and are one of the strongest and most consistent predictors of environmental and humanitarian actions, which is why this study uses values to represent motivation (Schwartz, 2012). Because values are higher-order, abstract predictors that shape other psychological determinants of environmental behavior (Bouman et al., 2021), the inclusion model may apply best to such abstract, broad motivations. Surveying the literature, we find some piecemeal evidence for an inclusion pattern with connectedness with nature (see Neaman et al., 2023; Otto et al., 2021). We expect that being more connected with nature may mean being more connected with other people. However, we have not tested this conjecture and it remains an area for future research.

In contrast, we expect that the inclusion model does not extend to more concrete and context-dependent forms of motivation. With more proximal predictors of environmental behavior, such as self-and social identity, or more contextually rooted determinants, such as specific attitudes, the inclusion model seems less relevant. The inclusion model also does not apply to situations that create conflict between biospheric and altruistic motivations, as tradeoff research shows (e.g., Conte et al., 2021). When in conflict, it seems that whichever value is stronger and more relevant to the outcome wins out. More generally, whether the inclusion model plays out in behavior likely depends on the specific behavior in question. For instance, the inclusion model should apply to environmental outcomes that people also perceive as particularly instrumental in achieving biospheric goals. If an individual perceives an environmentally beneficial behavior as primarily altruistic, they may act primarily for altruistic reasons (see Neef et al., 2024).

For conducting research, the inclusion model offers a way to address interpretational challenges arising from the overlap between altruistic and biospheric values (e.g., suppression effects) through theory-driven bifactor modeling (see Section 3.4). More broadly, the inclusion model sheds new light on how researchers typically interpret findings on biospheric values. Prior work treats altruistic and biospheric values as correlated constructs and tests which better predicts environmental or humanitarian outcomes. Such work often links environmental outcomes more closely to how people value the natural world than to how people value other humans (see Bouman et al., 2021). However, this conclusion presupposes that biospheric values capture only how people value the natural world. If biospheric values contain both a biospheric-specific element and an altruistic core, observed association with outcomes may also reflect a mix of both elements (see Figure 5). Earlier findings deserve another look through this lens. If the inclusion model is taken seriously, altruistic and biospheric values should be modeled accordinglywith bifactor-(S-1) modelswhen predicting outcomes in the future.

4.3 Limitations and future research

Some limitations of our work deserve note. First, all data were cross-sectional. This is not an issue for co-occurrence patterns, but predictive models should not be interpreted as causal evidence. Second, in Studies 1 and 2, a score of 6 or higher indicated value endorsement, while a score below 6 indicated no endorsement. This dichotomization was done to confidently classify someone as holding strong values. Yet, dichotomization can amplify small-scale differences. A person scoring marginally below our threshold of 6 for altruistic values (e.g., 5) while meeting the threshold of 6 for biospheric values (e.g., 6) was counted as endorsing only biospheric values. Nevertheless, our results remained largely consistent across several alternative thresholds (see Table S.5). In addition, Study 3 relied upon single-and two-item proxy measures for altruistic and biospheric values that were included in WVS and ESS data. Others have also used the selected items as proxies (e.g., Law et al., 2025). Still, the global results of Study 3 should be interpreted with caution, and further corroboration with established scales is needed.

Third, it could be argued that our findings partly reflect a measurement artifact. An individual may endorse a biospheric value (e.g., "protecting the environment" as a life principle) for humanitarian reasons. Yet this underscores the inclusion model's purpose of highlighting how social and environmental values are intertwined. In the inclusion model, people are expected to endorse strong biospheric values out of concern for the planet and the people who are part of it. Indeed, this reasoning underlies the bifactor model, which separates biospheric values into altruistic and biospheric parts.

To examine whether the inclusion pattern still holds when human-oriented concern is separated from nature-oriented concern already in a questionnaire, we turned to Schultz's (2001) environmental concern scale (administered in Study 1). This scale distinguishes altruistic from biospheric environmental concern as its items refer to different entities affected by environmental problems (e.g., "all people" vs. "plants"). We found largely the same inclusion pattern as with values. Both the asymmetric co-occurrence pattern and the bifactor-(S-1) structure were replicated, though the predictive asymmetry was not (see Table S.1). This suggests that the inclusion pattern may be more fundamentally related to the structure of altruistic and biospheric concern than the result of a measurement artifact.

Finally, even though the asymmetric co-occurrence pattern largely held across the three studies, there seems to exist a proportion of participantsof varying size across studies and countriesthat exclusively hold biospheric values. This (small) subgroup does not fit within the inclusion model and therefore seems all the more interesting to investigate further.

4.4 Implications for practice

Our findings offer practical implications for environmental communication. Climate and conservation messaging often falls short in motivating broad engagement (see Kusmanoff et al., 2020). Because people with strong biospheric values mostly also hold strong altruistic values (but not vice versa), appeals to altruistic values may reach a broader audience without losing biospherically motivated individuals (see Göckeritz et al., 2010; Klein, Horsten, & Hilbig, 2022). Conversely, because biospheric values include an altruistic core, appeals to biospheric values may encourage not only environmental but also humanitarian action (see Ardoin et al., 2018).

Against this background, our findings are also relevant to the debate in environmental policy on whether nature should be protected for its own sake or for humans' sake (e.g., Chan et al., 2016). Tallis and Lubchenco (2014) argue that these two rationales need not be in opposition. Our findings support their view at the individual, psychological level. People who strongly endorse biospheric values do not do so at the expense of altruistic values. Rather than choosing one rationale over the other, campaigns to foster environmental protection may benefit from merging altruistic and biospheric appeals, depending on whether they aim to reach a broad audience or to mobilize those who already care about environmental issues (see Bain et al., 2016; Kidd et al., 2019).

4.5 Conclusion

In the opening lines of this piece, we deliberately withheld some information. The Citarum River is being cleaned up. Since 2018, a broad coalition that includes the Indonesian government, the United Nations, and international non-profits has undertaken massive efforts to clean up the river (Baumgartner, 2024). Tackling the climate crisis and its negative social and environmental implications also requires motivating people to do work that extends beyond pure self-interest, to help others and the planet (Otto et al., 2014). How we think about the interrelatedness of biospheric and altruistic values helps us better understand how people approach environmental and social justice issues. In line with the inclusion model, caring about nature implies also caring about others. This means that for individuals, environmental and social concerns are often compatible. Effectively tackling environmental issues means emphasizing the interconnectedness of environmental and human well-being.
